headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress make Flowise→Goose interactions risky for leakage, conflicts, and unverified downstream actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Flowise can read/write uploaded files and server filesystem, while Goose reads/writes the user filesystem and can use MCP/extensions. If Flowise outputs attacker-controlled content into files that Goose later ingests, Goose may treat it as trusted instructions. The shared-file bridge is plausible, but not proven by docs alone, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF Flowise writes untrusted content into a file Goose later reads
IF Goose parses that file as instructions or tool input without provenance checks
mitigations: Store Flowise outputs in a separate directory Goose does not watch
Add a manual review step before Goose consumes Flowise-generated files
Disable automatic file ingestion in Goose for shared folders
Tag Flowise outputs with provenance metadata
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization or allowlist parsing between the agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Flowise touches chatflow inputs/outputs and uploaded files, and Goose touches source code and files in cwd. Both have broad network egress, so sensitive file contents can flow from a shared workspace into model providers or APIs. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace by default, but the filesystem overlap makes leakage plausible enough for medium.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory or uploaded-file set
IF either agent forwards file contents to configured model providers or APIs
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for Flowise and Goose
Remove secrets from any shared directory before either agent runs
Restrict Goose to a scratch repo with no sensitive files
Restrict Flowise uploads to non-sensitive test data
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent egress allowlists and DLP scanning

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Flowise can write the server filesystem and shares state via server datastore; Goose can write the user filesystem, modify git state, and shares state via filesystem. If both are aimed at the same mutable directory or repo, concurrent writes and git changes can collide without locking. Because the profiles expose overlapping write surfaces and no coordination primitive, high is warranted.
conditions: IF Flowise and Goose write to the same directory or repository
IF Goose performs git operations while Flowise writes files in that tree
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate writable directory
Pause one agent before the other edits the same repo
Avoid git operations while Flowise is active on shared files
Use filesystem locks around shared paths
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Flowise is a graph-based agent flow builder that can emit tool outputs, and Goose is a coding/ops agent with shell, subprocess, and MCP capabilities. If Goose consumes Flowise output as authoritative, a bad or malicious Flowise result can trigger real actions such as code edits or commands. The downstream authority and lack of built-in verification make high appropriate.
conditions: IF Goose uses Flowise output as a direct instruction source
IF Goose executes shell, subprocess, or MCP actions based on that output without verification
mitigations: Require Goose to verify Flowise outputs against a schema
Insert a human approval step before any Goose action
Limit Goose to read-only mode for Flowise-derived tasks
Log and diff Flowise outputs before execution
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Flowise handles chatflow inputs/outputs and uploaded files, while Goose handles source code and cwd files. The profiles do not state residency or certifications, so a compliance breach is not proven; however, if regulated data is placed in shared files, differing logging/retention or backend handling could create a mismatch. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in files or chatflows processed by both agents
IF their backend logging or retention policies differ for that data class
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Review each agent's retention settings before use
Use synthetic data for cross-agent workflows
Document which data classes each agent may touch
requires-engineering: align residency, retention, and deletion controls
